title: My family — endings you already know from the English "my" and "your"
goal: Name family members and their jobs with possessive endings, then discover that Hungarian has no verb "to have" at all.
bekal: ask about and state a job

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Családi fotó
dialogs.intro: Budi shows a photo of his family on his phone. Anna is curious.

lines.text: Ez a családom. Ez az apám, ez pedig az anyám.

notes: **This is the friendliest part of the whole course for an English speaker.** *ház* → *házam* (my house), *könyv* → *könyved* (your book), *család* → *családja* (his/her family). English uses separate words (*my*, *your*, *his*); Hungarian simply attaches the owner to the end of the noun. One word instead of two, and the endings are short and regular.

**Apa becomes apám, anya becomes anyám.** The vowels *a* and *e* at the end of a word always lengthen when an ending is added. You already met the same rule in the plural *alma* → *almák* in Unit 3, and it will come back with every ending from here on.

**Hungarian has no verb "to have".** *Van egy bátyám* literally means "there is an older-brother-of-mine". Ownership is built from two ingredients you already know: *van/nincs* from Unit 4, and the possessive ending from this unit. There is no third ingredient.

**Nekem nincs testvérem** contains *nekem* ("to me"), which could actually be dropped — the ending *-em* on *testvérem* already names the owner. *Nekem* is used for **emphasis**: "as for me, I have none". The full set of forms is given below.

**Testvér doesn't say gender, but the other words say age.** English has only *brother* and *sister*; Hungarian adds one more layer: older or younger. *báty* (older brother), *nővér* (older sister), *öcs* (younger brother), *húg* (younger sister). The general word for all of them: *testvér*.

grammars.title: Possessive endings — words ending in a consonant
body: Three examples at once, one for each vowel group. Notice that the pattern is identical; only the linking vowel changes.
after: **Some words insert a j in the "his/her" and "their" forms.** *könyv* → *könyv**e***, but *asztal* → *asztal**a***, and *kert* → *kert**je***. Unfortunately there is no truly tidy rule; this group is learned as you go. The good news is that picking wrong here is still fully understood.
**The article almost always comes along.** Hungarians say *a házam* (my house), not a bare *házam*. This habit matters because the article is what later decides the verb form in Unit 11.

grammars.title: Possessive endings — words ending in a vowel
body: Shorter, because no linking vowel is needed. All you have to remember is the lengthening of *a* and *e* at the end.
after: *Apa* and *anya* rebel in the "his/her" and "their" rows: the forms are *apja* and *anyja*, not *apája*. These two words are used far too often to avoid, so just memorize them.

**Possession of plural things** uses *-i-* before the ending: *könyveim* (my books), *szüleim* (my parents), *barátaim* (my friends). For A1, just recognize the form when you hear it; building it yourself can wait.

grammars.title: To have = there is + possessive ending
body: Since there is no verb "to have", Hungarian builds it from ingredients that already exist. The construction is always the same.
after: If you want to stress the owner, add the forms *nekem, neked, neki, nekünk, nektek, nekik* in front: *Nekem van kutyám* = "I'm the one who has a dog". Without emphasis, this part is dropped.
Notice that what goes plural is the **thing owned**, not the owner: *Vannak könyveim* = I have several books. When the thing is plural, *van* also turns into *vannak*.

blocks.text: The sibling words above are written directly with the "my" ending because that is the form you will really use. For other owners, swap the tail: *a bátyád* (your older brother), *a húga* (his/her younger sister).
*Foglalkozás* is the formal word for "occupation". In casual conversation people more often ask *Mit dolgozol?* — literally "what do you work?".
